question: Management accounting is best described as:

options.text: A statutory system of recording the transactions of the business, maintained only to satisfy the requirements of the Companies Act
The application of accounting techniques (financial, cost and statistical) to provide information for PLANNING, CONTROL and DECISION- MAKING by management
The preparation of the annual financial statements of the business for the shareholders and the Registrar

The audit of the cost records of the business by the cost auditor appointed under the Companies Act - and management accounting is nothing more than this statutory audit of cost records, done once a year for the Registrar

explanation: Management accounting serves internal users; it has no statutory format and uses both historical and future-oriented data.

revisionHistory.question: Management accounting is best described as:
options: A statutory system of recording transactions
The application of accounting techniques (financial, cost and statistical) to provide information for PLANNING, CONTROL and DECISION- MAKING by management
revisionHistory.explanation: Management accounting serves internal users; it has no statutory format and uses both historical and future-oriented data.

question: Management accounting information is primarily meant for:

options.text: Income-tax authorities
INTERNAL management at all levels
Creditors
Shareholders

explanation: Financial accounting serves external users; management accounting serves internal decision-makers.

question: Which is TRUE of management accounting?

options.text: It is OPTIONAL/FACULTATIVE - prepared as and when needed, using future-oriented and estimated data
It is COMPULSORY for all the companies registered under the Companies Act, 2013
It deals only with the past data of the business, and never with the future
It follows the GAAP strictly in every respect, just as financial accounting does

explanation: No statute mandates management accounting; its reports are tailor-made, frequent and forward-looking.

revisionHistory.question: Which is TRUE of management accounting?
options: It is OPTIONAL/FACULTATIVE - prepared as and when needed, using future-oriented and estimated data
It is COMPULSORY for all companies
It deals only with past data
revisionHistory.explanation: No statute mandates management accounting; its reports are tailor-made, frequent and forward-looking.

question: The MAIN tools and techniques of management accounting do NOT include:

options.text: Double-entry bookkeeping
Marginal costing and capital budgeting
Budgetary control and standard costing
Ratio analysis, fund flow and cash flow analysis

explanation: Double entry is the recording mechanism of financial accounting; MA borrows and analyses the resulting data.

question: Management accounting is broader than cost accounting because it:

options.text: Combines FINANCIAL accounting + COST accounting + statistical tools to serve managerial decisions
It deals only with the future costs of the business, and never with the past
It applies only to the service industries, and never to the manufacturing concerns
It ignores the cost data altogether, relying on the financial statements alone

explanation: Cost accounting is a subset; management accounting additionally uses financial statements, budgets, ratios and statistics.

revisionHistory.question: Management accounting is broader than cost accounting because it:
options: Combines FINANCIAL accounting + COST accounting + statistical tools to serve managerial decisions
revisionHistory.explanation: Cost accounting is a subset; management accounting additionally uses financial statements, budgets, ratios and statistics.

question: Which of the following is a CHARACTERISTIC of management accounting?

options.text: The reports are prepared only once a year, at the close of the financial year
The reports are always audited by the statutory auditor before they are used
Reports may be at ANY interval, for ANY segment, in ANY format suited to the decision
It deals only with monetary and financial data drawn from the accounting records of the firm

explanation: Flexibility of period, segment and format is the essence of MA; it also uses qualitative and non-monetary data.

revisionHistory.question: Which of the following is a CHARACTERISTIC of management accounting?
options: Reports are prepared only once a year
Reports may be at ANY interval, for ANY segment, in ANY format suited to the decision
It is concerned only with monetary data
revisionHistory.explanation: Flexibility of period, segment and format is the essence of MA; it also uses qualitative and non-monetary data.

question: The installation of a management accounting system is:

options.text: Compulsory under the Income-tax Act, 1961, for every assessee carrying on a business
Compulsory under the Companies Act, 2013, for every company registered under it
Required by SEBI for every listed company, as a condition of the listing
OPTIONAL - it depends on the management own appreciation of its utility

explanation: Unlike financial or (for specified industries) cost records, MA reporting has no legal mandate.

revisionHistory.question: The installation of a management accounting system is:
options: OPTIONAL - it depends on the management own appreciation of its utility
revisionHistory.explanation: Unlike financial or (for specified industries) cost records, MA reporting has no legal mandate.

question: The scope of management accounting includes all EXCEPT:

options.text: Tax planning and inventory control
Financial accounting and analysis
Cost accounting and budgetary control
STATUTORY audit of accounts

explanation: Audit is an independent attestation function; MA covers planning, control, decision analysis, reporting and tax planning.

question: Management accounting reports are generally:

options.text: Published in newspapers
CONFIDENTIAL internal documents, not published
Sent to shareholders
Filed with the Registrar of Companies

explanation: MA reports are internal and confidential; external users have no right to them.

question: The chief limitation of management accounting is that it:

options.text: It cannot use the future data of the business at all, being wholly confined to the past records of the concern
It is not recognised as a legitimate tool of management by the law
DEPENDS on the accuracy of financial and cost records and involves heavy cost and broad (not deep) coverage
It cannot show the segment data of the business at all, being wholly confined to the figures of the whole concern

explanation: MA conclusions are only as good as the underlying financial/cost records; other limits: costly, broad-based, prone to personal bias, evolutionary stage.

revisionHistory.question: The chief limitation of management accounting is that it:
options: DEPENDS on the accuracy of financial and cost records and involves heavy cost and broad (not deep) coverage
revisionHistory.explanation: MA conclusions are only as good as the underlying financial/cost records; other limits: costly, broad-based, prone to personal bias, evolutionary stage.

question: The term "management accounting" was FIRST formally used (in its modern sense) by:

options.text: The Anglo-American Council on Productivity team (1950) - popularising the use of accounting information for management
CIMA in the year 2000, at its London convention of the member bodies of the accountancy profession
The ICAI in the year 1949, at the time of its own establishment in India under the Act of Parliament
The SEC of the United States, in its regulations framed in the year 1934 after the crash

explanation: The 1950 Anglo-American productivity team report popularised management accounting; the ICPAI/ICWAI and CIMA later institutionalised it.

revisionHistory.question: The term "management accounting" was FIRST formally used (in its modern sense) by:
options: The Anglo-American Council on Productivity team (1950) - popularising the use of accounting information for management
revisionHistory.explanation: The 1950 Anglo-American productivity team report popularised management accounting; the ICPAI/ICWAI and CIMA later institutionalised it.

question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of management accounting?

options.text: Coordinating and decision-making
Maintaining the statutory books of account
Controlling operations through budgets and standards
Planning and policy formulation

explanation: Statutory record-keeping is financial accounting; MA objectives are planning, organising, coordinating, motivating, communicating and controlling.

question: Management accounting is concerned with:

options.text: Only the whole enterprise as a single unit, and never its segments at all
Only the external reporting of the enterprise, and never the internal needs
Only the factory floor of the enterprise, and never the office or the market
The enterprise AS A WHOLE AND ITS SEGMENTS - departments, products, territories

explanation: Segment reporting (division, product line, region) is a hallmark of MA.

revisionHistory.question: Management accounting is concerned with:
options: The enterprise AS A WHOLE AND ITS SEGMENTS - departments, products, territories
revisionHistory.explanation: Segment reporting (division, product line, region) is a hallmark of MA.

question: The PRIMARY emphasis of management accounting is on:

options.text: The historical recording of the transactions of the business, day by day
FUTURE planning and decision-making (though it analyses past data)
The audit of the accounts of the business, as required by the statute
The tax compliance of the business, as required by the Income-tax Act

explanation: MA is forward-looking: budgets, forecasts, project appraisal and what-if analysis dominate.

revisionHistory.question: The PRIMARY emphasis of management accounting is on:
options: FUTURE planning and decision-making (though it analyses past data)
revisionHistory.explanation: MA is forward-looking: budgets, forecasts, project appraisal and what-if analysis dominate.

question: A management accountant in India is professionally associated with:

options.text: The ICSI - the Institute of Company Secretaries of India
The Institute of COST ACCOUNTANTS of India (ICMAI)
The RBI - the central bank of the country
The ICAI - the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India

explanation: Cost and management accountants are regulated by the ICMAI (formerly ICWAI); the qualification is CMA.

revisionHistory.question: A management accountant in India is professionally associated with:
options: The Institute of COST ACCOUNTANTS of India (ICMAI)
revisionHistory.explanation: Cost and management accountants are regulated by the ICMAI (formerly ICWAI); the qualification is CMA.

question: Which statement distinguishes management accounting from FINANCIAL accounting?

options.text: The financial accounting has no rules at all, while the management accounting follows GAAP strictly
FA is mandatory and historical/external; MA is optional, analytical, internal and future-oriented
The management accounting uses only the cash basis of accounting, while the financial accounting uses the accrual
The management accounting reports to SEBI directly, while the financial accounting reports to the shareholders

explanation: Financial accounting = stewardship + external reporting under GAAP/statute; management accounting = internal decision support.

revisionHistory.question: Which statement distinguishes management accounting from FINANCIAL accounting?
options: FA is mandatory and historical/external; MA is optional, analytical, internal and future-oriented
revisionHistory.explanation: Financial accounting = stewardship + external reporting under GAAP/statute; management accounting = internal decision support.

question: Which statement distinguishes management accounting from COST accounting?

options.text: The cost accounting covers the whole information system of the business, while the management accounting covers only a part
They are identical in every respect, being two names for the same discipline
Cost accounting RECORDS and analyses costs; management accounting ADDITIONALLY uses financial data and other tools for decisions
The cost accounting is external in its orientation, while the management accounting is internal

explanation: Cost accounting feeds cost data into the wider MA system; MA uses cost + financial + statistical data.

revisionHistory.question: Which statement distinguishes management accounting from COST accounting?
options: Cost accounting covers the whole information system
Cost accounting RECORDS and analyses costs; management accounting ADDITIONALLY uses financial data and other tools for decisions
revisionHistory.explanation: Cost accounting feeds cost data into the wider MA system; MA uses cost + financial + statistical data.

question: Responsibility accounting, a part of management accounting, means:

options.text: The government accounting of the departments, as practised by the CAG of India
Assigning costs/revenues to RESPONSIBILITY CENTRES headed by managers accountable for them
The accounting for the social responsibility of the business, as required by the Companies Act
The accounting only for the owners of the business, and for no one else at all

explanation: Responsibility centres (cost, revenue, profit, investment centres) pin performance to the manager who controls it.

revisionHistory.question: Responsibility accounting, a part of management accounting, means:
options: Assigning costs/revenues to RESPONSIBILITY CENTRES headed by managers accountable for them
revisionHistory.explanation: Responsibility centres (cost, revenue, profit, investment centres) pin performance to the manager who controls it.

question: The information supplied by management accounting should be:

options.text: Only the audited figures, however late they may be available to the managers
Always rounded to lakhs
Always rounded to the lakhs, so that the managers are not confused by the detail
APPROXIMATE BUT TIMELY - relevance and speed matter more than exact precision

explanation: MA accepts approximate figures prepared quickly; delayed precision has no decision value.

revisionHistory.question: The information supplied by management accounting should be:
options: APPROXIMATE BUT TIMELY - relevance and speed matter more than exact precision
revisionHistory.explanation: MA accepts approximate figures prepared quickly; delayed precision has no decision value.

question: Which of the following pairs are BOTH techniques of management accounting?

options.text: Trial balance and journal
Bank reconciliation and audit
Ratio analysis and cash flow analysis
Ledger posting and vouching

explanation: Ratio analysis and fund/cash flow analysis are core MA analytical tools; the others are bookkeeping/audit processes.

question: Ratio analysis is a technique of:

options.text: The preparation of the vouchers of the business, as the first step of the accounting work
Analysing and INTERPRETING financial statements by establishing mathematical relationships between related figures
The physical verification of the assets of the business, as the auditor does at the year end
The recording of the transactions of the business in the books of prime entry, day by day

explanation: A ratio expresses one figure as a quotient/percentage/proportion of another; its value lies in comparison with standards, past periods or other firms.

revisionHistory.question: Ratio analysis is a technique of:
options: Analysing and INTERPRETING financial statements by establishing mathematical relationships between related figures
revisionHistory.explanation: A ratio expresses one figure as a quotient/percentage/proportion of another; its value lies in comparison with standards, past periods or other firms.

question: Ratios are broadly classified (traditional/functional classification) into:

options.text: LIQUIDITY, SOLVENCY (leverage/capital structure), ACTIVITY (turnover) and PROFITABILITY ratios
Only the profitability ratios, since profit alone matters to every user of the statements
Only the liquidity ratios, since the payment of debts alone matters to every user
The primary and the secondary ratios only, under the traditional classification of ratios

explanation: The functional classification groups ratios by the aspect they test: short-term liquidity, long-term solvency, efficiency of asset use, and profitability.

revisionHistory.question: Ratios are broadly classified (traditional/functional classification) into:
options: LIQUIDITY, SOLVENCY (leverage/capital structure), ACTIVITY (turnover) and PROFITABILITY ratios
revisionHistory.explanation: The functional classification groups ratios by the aspect they test: short-term liquidity, long-term solvency, efficiency of asset use, and profitability.

question: The CURRENT RATIO is computed as:

options.text: Current liabilities / Current assets
CURRENT ASSETS / CURRENT LIABILITIES
Quick assets / Current liabilities
Debt / Equity

explanation: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities; the conventional yardstick is 2:1, though industry norms vary.

question: CURRENT ASSETS include all EXCEPT:

options.text: Stock/inventory and debtors
PRELIMINARY EXPENSES not written off
Bills receivable and prepaid expenses
Cash, bank and short-term investments

explanation: Fictitious/deferred assets (preliminary expenses, discount on issue of shares) are NOT current assets - they cannot be converted to cash.

question: CURRENT LIABILITIES include:

options.text: Outstanding expenses, sundry creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft and short-term loans
The general reserve of the company, built out of the profits of the earlier years
The share capital of the company, contributed by the shareholders of the company
The long-term loans of the company, repayable after the period of five years

explanation: Current liabilities are obligations payable within a year (or the operating cycle), including provisions like provision for tax and proposed dividend.

revisionHistory.question: CURRENT LIABILITIES include:
options: Outstanding expenses, sundry creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft and short-term loans
revisionHistory.explanation: Current liabilities are obligations payable within a year (or the operating cycle), including provisions like provision for tax and proposed dividend.

question: The IDEAL current ratio traditionally regarded as satisfactory is:
explanation: The 2:1 rule of thumb gives a safety margin on realisation of current assets; a very high ratio may indicate idle funds or poor working-capital management.

question: The QUICK (acid-test/liquid) ratio is:

options.text: The total debt of the company divided by the equity of the company, as the solvency test
The current assets of the company divided by the current liabilities, as the solvency test
The stock of the company divided by the debtors of the company, as the solvency test
QUICK ASSETS (current assets minus stock and prepaid expenses) / CURRENT LIABILITIES

explanation: Quick ratio excludes inventory and prepaid expenses because they convert to cash slowly; the yardstick is 1:1.

revisionHistory.question: The QUICK (acid-test/liquid) ratio is:
options: QUICK ASSETS (current assets minus stock and prepaid expenses) / CURRENT LIABILITIES
revisionHistory.explanation: Quick ratio excludes inventory and prepaid expenses because they convert to cash slowly; the yardstick is 1:1.

question: Quick liabilities EXCLUDE:

options.text: The sundry creditors of the business - quick liabilities exclude every kind of creditor of the concern
The bills payable of the business - quick liabilities exclude every kind of acceptance of the concern
The outstanding expenses of the business - quick liabilities exclude every accrued charge of the concern
BANK OVERDRAFT - quick liabilities = current liabilities minus bank overdraft (it is treated as a semi-permanent source)

explanation: The usual formula: quick ratio = quick assets / (current liabilities - bank overdraft). Bank overdraft is excluded from quick liabilities because it is a continuing source of finance.

revisionHistory.question: Quick liabilities EXCLUDE:
options: BANK OVERDRAFT - quick liabilities = current liabilities minus bank overdraft (it is treated as a semi-permanent source)
revisionHistory.explanation: The usual formula: quick ratio = quick assets / (current liabilities - bank overdraft). Bank overdraft is excluded from quick liabilities because it is a continuing source of finance.

question: The ideal quick (acid-test) ratio is:
explanation: A 1:1 acid-test ratio means immediately realisable assets cover immediate liabilities fully.

question: A firm has current assets of Rs.4,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs.2,00,000. Its current ratio is:
A firm has current assets Rs.3,00,000 (including stock Rs.1,00,000 and prepaid expenses Rs.20,000) and current liabilities Rs.1,50,000 (including bank overdraft Rs.30,000). Its QUICK ratio is:
When the current ratio is 2:1 and there is an EQUAL increase in current assets and current liabilities, the ratio will:

options.text: Become zero
Increase
Remain unchanged
DECREASE

explanation: Adding equal amounts to both sides of a ratio greater than 1 pulls it down toward 1 (e.g. 2:1 plus 0.5/0.5 becomes 2.5:1.5 = 1.67:1).

question: Payment of a CURRENT LIABILITY in cash will:

options.text: Reduce the working capital of the business, since the cash goes out of it
IMPROVE (increase) the current ratio when it is above 1
Decrease the current ratio of the business, when the ratio is already above one
Leave the current ratio of the business unchanged always, whatever the payment

explanation: Equal reduction of CA and CL raises a ratio that is above 1 (e.g. CA 4, CL 2, paying 1 in cash leaves 3/1 = 3:1); total working capital stays unchanged.

revisionHistory.question: Payment of a CURRENT LIABILITY in cash will:
options: IMPROVE (increase) the current ratio when it is above 1
revisionHistory.explanation: Equal reduction of CA and CL raises a ratio that is above 1 (e.g. CA 4, CL 2, paying 1 in cash leaves 3/1 = 3:1); total working capital stays unchanged.

question: Purchase of stock-in-trade on CREDIT will:

options.text: Improve the quick ratio of the business at once, since the stock is a quick asset of the business itself
Decrease the working capital of the business at once, since the stock comes into the business on credit terms
INCREASE current assets and current liabilities EQUALLY - the current ratio FALLS if it was above 1; working capital stays UNCHANGED
Increase the working capital of the business at once, since the stock comes into the business itself at once

explanation: Credit purchases add equal amounts to stock (CA) and creditors (CL): working capital unchanged, current ratio moves toward 1.

revisionHistory.question: Purchase of stock-in-trade on CREDIT will:
options: INCREASE current assets and current liabilities EQUALLY - the current ratio FALLS if it was above 1; working capital stays UNCHANGED
revisionHistory.explanation: Credit purchases add equal amounts to stock (CA) and creditors (CL): working capital unchanged, current ratio moves toward 1.

question: The ABSOLUTE liquid (cash) ratio is:

options.text: The debtors of the business divided by the sales of the year, as the liquidity test
The current assets of the business divided by the current liabilities, as the liquidity test
(Cash + bank + marketable securities) / Current liabilities
The cash of the business divided by the total assets of the business, as the liquidity test

explanation: The cash ratio tests immediate solvency with cash and near-cash only; 0.5:1 is the commonly cited norm.

revisionHistory.question: The ABSOLUTE liquid (cash) ratio is:
revisionHistory.explanation: The cash ratio tests immediate solvency with cash and near-cash only; 0.5:1 is the commonly cited norm.

question: DEBT-EQUITY ratio is computed as:

options.text: The fixed assets of the company divided by the equity of the company
LONG-TERM DEBT / SHAREHOLDERS FUNDS (outsiders funds / own funds)
The equity of the company divided by the debt of the company
The total debt of the company divided by the current liabilities of the company

explanation: Debt-equity = long-term external liabilities / shareholders funds; the conventional comfortable norm is 2:1 (varies by industry).

revisionHistory.question: DEBT-EQUITY ratio is computed as:
options: LONG-TERM DEBT / SHAREHOLDERS FUNDS (outsiders funds / own funds)
revisionHistory.explanation: Debt-equity = long-term external liabilities / shareholders funds; the conventional comfortable norm is 2:1 (varies by industry).

question: Shareholders funds (proprietors funds/own funds) equal:

options.text: The share capital of the company taken by itself alone, with nothing added to it
The fixed assets of the company, at their written-down value
Share capital + RESERVES AND SURPLUS - accumulated losses and fictitious assets
The total assets of the company, at their balance-sheet values

explanation: Own funds = paid-up capital (equity + preference, as defined) plus free reserves minus accumulated losses, preliminary expenses and other fictitious assets.

revisionHistory.question: Shareholders funds (proprietors funds/own funds) equal:
options: Share capital + RESERVES AND SURPLUS - accumulated losses and fictitious assets
revisionHistory.explanation: Own funds = paid-up capital (equity + preference, as defined) plus free reserves minus accumulated losses, preliminary expenses and other fictitious assets.

question: The PROPRIETARY ratio is:

options.text: Proprietors funds / TOTAL ASSETS
Debt / Equity
Current assets / Total assets
Net profit / Sales

explanation: Proprietary ratio = shareholders funds / total assets; higher values indicate a stronger long-term financial position. A 0.5:1 or higher level is considered adequate.

question: The SOLVENCY ratio (total liabilities to total assets) indicates:

options.text: The profitability of the business, since the ratio compares the profit with the assets of the concern
The liquidity of the business, since the ratio compares the cash with the debts of the concern
The extent to which total assets are financed by OUTSIDERS liabilities - lower ratio means better long-term solvency
The activity of the business, since the ratio compares the sales with the assets of the concern

explanation: Solvency ratio = total outside liabilities / total assets; it is the inverse view of the proprietary ratio.

revisionHistory.question: The SOLVENCY ratio (total liabilities to total assets) indicates:
options: The extent to which total assets are financed by OUTSIDERS liabilities - lower ratio means better long-term solvency
revisionHistory.explanation: Solvency ratio = total outside liabilities / total assets; it is the inverse view of the proprietary ratio.

question: Which of the following is also termed a LEVERAGE ratio?

options.text: Current ratio
DEBT-EQUITY ratio
Gross profit ratio
Stock turnover ratio

explanation: Capital-structure (leverage) ratios - debt-equity, proprietary, capital-gearing - measure the mix of debt and equity.

question: The CAPITAL GEARING ratio is:

options.text: The sales of the year divided by the capital employed in the business
The debt of the company divided by the total assets of the company
The profit of the year divided by the equity of the company
(Equity share capital + free reserves) / FIXED-INTEREST/DIVIDEND bearing securities

explanation: Capital gearing compares equity funds to fixed-return funds (preference capital + debt); a high ratio = low gearing (conservative), low ratio = high gearing (trading on equity).

revisionHistory.question: The CAPITAL GEARING ratio is:
options: (Equity share capital + free reserves) / FIXED-INTEREST/DIVIDEND bearing securities
revisionHistory.explanation: Capital gearing compares equity funds to fixed-return funds (preference capital + debt); a high ratio = low gearing (conservative), low ratio = high gearing (trading on equity).

question: FIXED ASSETS ratio is:

options.text: Fixed assets / Equity share capital only
Fixed assets / LONG-TERM FUNDS (capital employed)
Fixed assets / Sales
Fixed assets / Current assets

explanation: Fixed assets / long-term funds shows whether fixed assets are financed by long-term money; ideally it should not exceed 1.

question: The INTEREST COVERAGE (debt service) ratio is:

options.text: Sales / Interest
EBIT / Tax
Net profit / Interest
EBIT / FIXED INTEREST CHARGES

explanation: Interest coverage = earnings before interest and tax / interest; it shows how many times earnings cover the interest burden (7x is a common comfort level).

question: DIVIDEND coverage (preference) ratio is:

options.text: NPAT / PREFERENCE DIVIDEND
Dividend / Profit
Equity dividend / NPAT
Dividend / Sales

explanation: Preference dividend cover = net profit after tax / preference dividend; for equity dividend, NPAT minus preference dividend over equity dividend.

question: The DEBT SERVICE COVERAGE ratio (DSCR) is:

options.text: The cash of the business divided by the total debt of the business, as the coverage test
EBIT divided by the interest payable for the year, the principal instalments of the loans being ignored altogether
The sales of the year divided by the total debt of the business, as the coverage test
(Net profit after tax + depreciation + interest on long-term loans) / (interest + PRINCIPAL instalments due)

explanation: DSCR measures the cash available to service both interest and principal; lenders look for 1.5-2x.

revisionHistory.question: The DEBT SERVICE COVERAGE ratio (DSCR) is:
options: (Net profit after tax + depreciation + interest on long-term loans) / (interest + PRINCIPAL instalments due)
revisionHistory.explanation: DSCR measures the cash available to service both interest and principal; lenders look for 1.5-2x.

question: Trading on EQUITY (financial leverage) is beneficial when:

options.text: The equity of the company is nil, so that the whole capital is debt
The RATE OF RETURN ON CAPITAL EMPLOYED exceeds the rate of interest on debt
The interest rates rise in the market, so that the debt becomes dearer
The cost of the debt exceeds the return on the capital employed in the business

explanation: When ROI > interest rate, the surplus on borrowed funds accrues to equity shareholders, magnifying their return.

revisionHistory.question: Trading on EQUITY (financial leverage) is beneficial when:
options: The RATE OF RETURN ON CAPITAL EMPLOYED exceeds the rate of interest on debt
Cost of debt exceeds the return on capital employed
revisionHistory.explanation: When ROI > interest rate, the surplus on borrowed funds accrues to equity shareholders, magnifying their return.

question: A high debt-equity ratio indicates:

options.text: A risky capital structure - higher fixed interest burden and lower cushion for lenders
A low gearing of the capital structure, with a small burden of the fixed interest
A low risk to the lenders, with a large cushion of the own funds for them
A high liquidity of the business, with a large holding of the quick assets

explanation: High leverage magnifies both gains and losses and raises financial risk; lenders prefer a lower ratio.

revisionHistory.question: A high debt-equity ratio indicates:
options: A risky capital structure - higher fixed interest burden and lower cushion for lenders
revisionHistory.explanation: High leverage magnifies both gains and losses and raises financial risk; lenders prefer a lower ratio.

question: Which group of ratios is primarily of interest to SHORT-TERM creditors?

options.text: The profitability ratios, since the creditors lend only to the profitable concerns
LIQUIDITY ratios (current, quick, cash)
The return on the equity, since the creditors lend only to the high-return concerns
The capital gearing of the company, since the creditors lend only to the low-geared concerns

explanation: Short-term lenders and suppliers judge repayment ability through liquidity ratios and the working-capital position.

revisionHistory.question: Which group of ratios is primarily of interest to SHORT-TERM creditors?
revisionHistory.explanation: Short-term lenders and suppliers judge repayment ability through liquidity ratios and the working-capital position.

question: Which group of ratios is primarily of interest to LONG-TERM lenders (debenture holders, term lenders)?

options.text: The operating ratio, since the lenders lend only to the low-cost concerns
The liquidity ratios, since the lenders look only to the payment of the current debts
The turnover ratios, since the lenders look only to the speed of the cycle
SOLVENCY/leverage ratios plus interest and debt-service coverage

explanation: Long-term lenders focus on capital structure, asset cover and debt-servicing capacity.

revisionHistory.question: Which group of ratios is primarily of interest to LONG-TERM lenders (debenture holders, term lenders)?
options: SOLVENCY/leverage ratios plus interest and debt-service coverage
revisionHistory.explanation: Long-term lenders focus on capital structure, asset cover and debt-servicing capacity.

question: The basic LIMITATION of ratio analysis does NOT include:

options.text: Ratios are based on historical data and ignore price-level changes
Different firms use different accounting policies, hurting comparability
Ratios are affected by window dressing
Ratios give ABSOLUTE answers that need no interpretation

explanation: Ratios are only indicators needing interpretation against standards, trends and industry - they never speak absolutely.

question: A current ratio that is TOO HIGH (say 6:1) usually indicates:

options.text: IDLE funds, over-stocking or poor collection - inefficient working-capital use
An excellent management of the working capital of the business, and nothing wrong at all
A high profitability of the business, since the ratio rises with the profit
A certain bankruptcy of the business, since the ratio can never be too high

explanation: Excessive liquidity signals unutilised resources; ratios must be judged against the industry norm, not merely maximised.

revisionHistory.question: A current ratio that is TOO HIGH (say 6:1) usually indicates:
options: IDLE funds, over-stocking or poor collection - inefficient working-capital use
revisionHistory.explanation: Excessive liquidity signals unutilised resources; ratios must be judged against the industry norm, not merely maximised.

question: Window dressing in financial statements:

options.text: DISTORTS ratios (e.g. paying creditors just before the balance sheet date to inflate the current ratio)
Improves the reliability of the ratios computed from the statements, for every user of them
Is illegal under the law but harmless to every user of the financial statements
Affects only the profit of the year, and never the ratios of the business at all

explanation: Cosmetic period-end adjustments can flatter liquidity and other ratios; analysts should use averages and audit-adjusted data.

revisionHistory.question: Window dressing in financial statements:

explanation: Writing off intangibles is a book entry with no working-capital effect; it is added back.

revisionHistory.question: Goodwill WRITTEN OFF is:
options: ADDED BACK to profit in FFO computation (non-fund item)
revisionHistory.explanation: Writing off intangibles is a book entry with no working-capital effect; it is added back.

question: Profit on sale of a FIXED ASSET is:

options.text: Treated as the depreciation of the year, and handled exactly like it in the computation
Added to the profit in the FFO computation, as a non-fund credit of the year
An application of the funds of the business, shown on the uses side of the statement
SUBTRACTED from profit in FFO computation; the full sale PROCEEDS are shown separately as a source

explanation: Only the total proceeds are a source; the profit element inside them is non-operating and is removed from FFO.

revisionHistory.question: Profit on sale of a FIXED ASSET is:
options: SUBTRACTED from profit in FFO computation; the full sale PROCEEDS are shown separately as a source
revisionHistory.explanation: Only the total proceeds are a source; the profit element inside them is non-operating and is removed from FFO.

question: LOSS on sale of a fixed asset is:

options.text: An application of the funds of the business, shown on the uses side
Ignored altogether in the fund flow analysis, as a mere book entry
Subtracted from the profit in the FFO computation, as a non-fund debit
Added back in FFO; the sale proceeds appear as a source

explanation: The book loss is non-operating (added back); the actual proceeds are a source of funds.

revisionHistory.question: LOSS on sale of a fixed asset is:
options: Added back in FFO; the sale proceeds appear as a source
revisionHistory.explanation: The book loss is non-operating (added back); the actual proceeds are a source of funds.

question: The SCHEDULE OF CHANGES IN WORKING CAPITAL shows:

options.text: The cash flows of the business between the two dates
The movement in the reserves between the two dates
The increase/decrease in EACH current asset and current liability and the net change in working capital between two dates
The sources from which funds came between the two dates

explanation: An increase in current assets increases working capital; an increase in current liabilities decreases it; the schedule nets these out.

revisionHistory.question: The SCHEDULE OF CHANGES IN WORKING CAPITAL shows:
options: The increase/decrease in EACH current asset and current liability and the net change in working capital between two dates
revisionHistory.explanation: An increase in current assets increases working capital; an increase in current liabilities decreases it; the schedule nets these out.

question: While preparing the schedule of changes in working capital:

options.text: Both increases raise the working capital of the business, whether of current assets or of current liabilities in the period
Both increases lower the working capital of the business
The current liabilities never affect the working capital of the business at all, whatever
An increase in current assets increases working capital; an increase in current liabilities DECREASES it

explanation: WC = CA - CL: rising CA raises WC, rising CL lowers it - the first rule of the schedule.

revisionHistory.question: While preparing the schedule of changes in working capital:
options: An increase in current assets increases working capital; an increase in current liabilities DECREASES it
revisionHistory.explanation: WC = CA - CL: rising CA raises WC, rising CL lowers it - the first rule of the schedule.

question: Provision for taxation and proposed dividend, in fund flow analysis, are usually treated as:

options.text: Current liabilities in the schedule of changes in working capital prepared for the year
Ignored altogether in the fund flow analysis, as mere book entries
NON-CURRENT items - tax PAID and dividend PAID are shown as APPLICATIONS of funds
Sources of the funds of the business, shown on the sources side of the statement

explanation: Under the preferred treatment they are kept out of the current schedule; additions are adjusted in FFO and payments shown as applications.

revisionHistory.question: Provision for taxation and proposed dividend, in fund flow analysis, are usually treated as:
options: NON-CURRENT items - tax PAID and dividend PAID are shown as APPLICATIONS of funds
revisionHistory.explanation: Under the preferred treatment they are kept out of the current schedule; additions are adjusted in FFO and payments shown as applications.

question: A fund flow statement is:

options.text: An audited statement, certified by the statutory auditor of the company every year without fail
NOT mandatory - a supplementary analytical statement (the Companies Act requires the CASH flow statement instead)
A legal requirement under the Companies Act, 2013, for every company registered under that Act
A part of the balance sheet of the company, presented along with it every year to the Registrar

explanation: Only cash flow statements (AS-3) are prescribed; the fund flow statement is an internal/voluntary analysis.

revisionHistory.question: A fund flow statement is:
options: NOT mandatory - a supplementary analytical statement (the Companies Act requires the CASH flow statement instead)
A legal requirement under the Companies Act
revisionHistory.explanation: Only cash flow statements (AS-3) are prescribed; the fund flow statement is an internal/voluntary analysis.

question: The net result of a fund flow statement (sources vs applications) equals:

options.text: The increase or decrease in WORKING CAPITAL shown by the schedule of changes
The net profit of the year, as shown in the statement of profit and loss
The reserves of the company, as shown in the balance sheet
The cash balance of the business, as shown in the balance sheet

explanation: Sources minus applications must reconcile with the net working-capital change from the schedule - the statement is self-balancing.

revisionHistory.question: The net result of a fund flow statement (sources vs applications) equals:
options: The increase or decrease in WORKING CAPITAL shown by the schedule of changes
revisionHistory.explanation: Sources minus applications must reconcile with the net working-capital change from the schedule - the statement is self-balancing.

question: Provision for depreciation on machinery increases during the year by Rs.50,000 while machinery is sold with accumulated depreciation Rs.20,000. Depreciation charged for the year is:
explanation: Closing provision = opening + charge for year - provision on asset sold: charge = 50,000 (net rise) + 20,000 (removed) = Rs.70,000.

question: Dividend RECEIVED on investments is:

options.text: A non-operating income SUBTRACTED from FFO (it is shown, if significant, separately as inflow or netted)
An application of the funds of the business
Added to the profit in the FFO computation, as an operating income of the year of receipt
A part of the operating income of the business and so it is included in the funds from operations of the year

explanation: Investment income is non-operating for a non-investment business and is excluded from FFO.

revisionHistory.question: Dividend RECEIVED on investments is:
options: A non-operating income SUBTRACTED from FFO (it is shown, if significant, separately as inflow or netted)
revisionHistory.explanation: Investment income is non-operating for a non-investment business and is excluded from FFO.

question: Fund flow statement is also known as the statement of:

options.text: SOURCES AND APPLICATIONS OF FUNDS / statement of changes in financial position
The retained earnings of the company, year after year, as the other name
The cash receipts and payments of the business, during the year, as the other name
The profit appropriation of the company, during the year, as the other name

explanation: Its classic title is "Statement of Sources and Application of Funds" or "Statement of Changes in Financial Position (working capital basis)".

revisionHistory.question: Fund flow statement is also known as the statement of:
options: SOURCES AND APPLICATIONS OF FUNDS / statement of changes in financial position
revisionHistory.explanation: Its classic title is "Statement of Sources and Application of Funds" or "Statement of Changes in Financial Position (working capital basis)".

question: Transfer to GENERAL RESERVE out of profits is:

options.text: Ignored altogether in the fund flow analysis, as a mere book entry of the year
An application of the funds of the business, shown on the uses side of the statement
A source of the funds of the business, shown on the sources side of the statement
ADDED BACK to current-year profit in the FFO computation (an appropriation, not a fund use)

explanation: Transfers to reserves merely move profit within equity; no working capital leaves the business.

revisionHistory.question: Transfer to GENERAL RESERVE out of profits is:
options: ADDED BACK to current-year profit in the FFO computation (an appropriation, not a fund use)
revisionHistory.explanation: Transfers to reserves merely move profit within equity; no working capital leaves the business.

question: Issue of BONUS shares is:

options.text: A NON-FUND transaction - a capitalisation of reserves with no working-capital effect
A source of the funds of the business, shown on the sources side of the statement
An application of the funds of the business, shown on the uses side of the statement
A cash inflow of the business, shown in the schedule of the changes

explanation: Bonus issue converts reserves into share capital; no fund flow arises.

revisionHistory.question: Issue of BONUS shares is:
options: A NON-FUND transaction - a capitalisation of reserves with no working-capital effect
revisionHistory.explanation: Bonus issue converts reserves into share capital; no fund flow arises.

question: Purchase of machinery by ISSUE OF EQUITY SHARES is:

options.text: A source of the funds of the business, since the shares are issued
An application of the funds of the business, since the machinery is bought
A NON-FUND transaction (both items non-current) - disclosed, if at all, separately
A fund inflow of the business, since the machinery comes in

explanation: No working capital moves; it is excluded from the fund flow statement.

revisionHistory.question: Purchase of machinery by ISSUE OF EQUITY SHARES is:
options: A NON-FUND transaction (both items non-current) - disclosed, if at all, separately
revisionHistory.explanation: No working capital moves; it is excluded from the fund flow statement.

question: The excess of applications over sources of funds indicates:

options.text: Higher cash always
Higher profit
Increase in working capital
DECREASE in working capital

explanation: When uses exceed sources, working capital falls - and the schedule will show the same net decrease.

question: A CASH FLOW statement (AS-3) classifies cash flows into:

options.text: The fixed and the variable flows of the cash of the business
OPERATING, INVESTING and FINANCING activities
The capital and the revenue flows of the cash of the business
The sources and the applications of the funds of the business

explanation: AS-3 mandates the three-way classification so users can see cash generated by operations, invested in assets, and raised/repaid through financing.

revisionHistory.question: A CASH FLOW statement (AS-3) classifies cash flows into:
revisionHistory.explanation: AS-3 mandates the three-way classification so users can see cash generated by operations, invested in assets, and raised/repaid through financing.

question: The "cash and cash equivalents" of AS-3 include:

options.text: The debtors of the business, as the most liquid of its assets
The long-term investments of the business, as the safest of its assets
CASH IN HAND and demand deposits + SHORT-TERM highly liquid investments (maturity up to 3 months) readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of value change

ALL the bank balances of the business including the fixed deposits for five years, the entire debtors of the business as the most liquid of its assets, and the long-term investments of the business as the safest of its assets - every one of these being a cash equivalent under AS-3

explanation: Cash equivalents are short-term (<=3 months from acquisition), highly liquid investments like T-bills and money-market instruments; bank overdrafts repayable on demand are treated as part of cash management.

revisionHistory.question: The "cash and cash equivalents" of AS-3 include:
options: CASH IN HAND and demand deposits + SHORT-TERM highly liquid investments (maturity up to 3 months) readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of value change
All bank balances including fixed deposits for 5 years
revisionHistory.explanation: Cash equivalents are short-term (<=3 months from acquisition), highly liquid investments like T-bills and money-market instruments; bank overdrafts repayable on demand are treated as part of cash management.

question: Which is an OPERATING activity?

options.text: The purchase of the machinery for the factory of the business, for cash, during the year under review
The purchase of the investments by the business, for cash, during the year under review

PAYMENT for the purchase of a machine, the purchase of the investments, the repayment of a bank loan, the proceeds from the issue of shares and debentures, and the payment of dividends - every one of these being an operating activity of the business under AS-3
Cash receipts from sale of goods and rendering of services; payments to suppliers and employees; income tax paid (unless specifically identified with investing/financing)

explanation: Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise.

revisionHistory.question: Which is an OPERATING activity?
options: Cash receipts from sale of goods and rendering of services; payments to suppliers and employees; income tax paid (unless specifically identified with investing/financing)
revisionHistory.explanation: Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise.

question: Which of the following is NOT an operating activity?

options.text: PAYMENT FOR PURCHASE OF A MACHINE (an INVESTING activity)
The payment of the rent of the premises of the business, for the year
The payment of the wages of the workers of the business, for the year
The cash received from the customers of the business, during the year

explanation: Acquisition of fixed assets is an investing activity; the recall question hinges exactly on this classification.

revisionHistory.question: Which of the following is NOT an operating activity?
options: PAYMENT FOR PURCHASE OF A MACHINE (an INVESTING activity)
revisionHistory.explanation: Acquisition of fixed assets is an investing activity; the recall question hinges exactly on this classification.

question: INCOME TAX paid is generally classified under:

options.text: Excluded from the statement altogether, since the tax is not a business flow
The financing activities of the business, since the tax is a cost of the capital
The investing activities of the business, since the tax is a cost of the assets
OPERATING activities - unless specifically identifiable with investing or financing activities

explanation: AS-3 defaults tax cash flows to operating; only taxes specifically attributable to investing/financing transactions follow those heads.

revisionHistory.question: INCOME TAX paid is generally classified under:
options: OPERATING activities - unless specifically identifiable with investing or financing activities
revisionHistory.explanation: AS-3 defaults tax cash flows to operating; only taxes specifically attributable to investing/financing transactions follow those heads.

question: Proceeds from the SALE OF A PATENT are classified as:

options.text: Operating activity
Financing activity
INVESTING activity
Cash equivalent

explanation: Disposal of intangible/fixed assets generates investing inflows.

question: Cash payment for a SELF-CONSTRUCTED property is classified as:

options.text: Either operating or financing
Financing activity
INVESTING activity
Operating activity

explanation: Payments to acquire or construct fixed assets are investing outflows.

question: Which is a FINANCING activity?

options.text: The purchase of the stock of the business, for cash or on credit
The payment of the wages of the workers of the business, for the year

PROCEEDS from the sale of the goods of the business, the cash received from the customers, the payments to the suppliers and the employees, and the income tax paid - every one of these being a financing activity of the business under AS-3
Repayment of a bank LOAN (principal), proceeds from issue of shares and debentures, payment of dividends and interest on borrowings (for non-financial enterprises, as per AS-3 options)

explanation: Financing activities change the size and composition of owners capital and borrowings.

revisionHistory.question: Which is a FINANCING activity?
options: Repayment of a bank LOAN (principal), proceeds from issue of shares and debentures, payment of dividends and interest on borrowings (for non-financial enterprises, as per AS-3 options)
revisionHistory.explanation: Financing activities change the size and composition of owners capital and borrowings.

question: For a NON-FINANCIAL enterprise under AS-3, INTEREST PAID is shown as:

options.text: FINANCING activity
Excluded
Operating
Investing

explanation: AS-3 allows interest paid as financing for non-financial enterprises; interest and dividends RECEIVED are investing; dividend PAID is financing. (For financial enterprises, interest paid and received are operating.)

question: DIVIDEND PAID by a company is classified as:

options.text: An operating activity of the business, since the dividend is an appropriation
FINANCING activity (it is a cost of obtaining financial resources)
An investing activity of the business, since the dividend relates to the shares
Not a cash flow at all, since the dividend is a mere appropriation of profit

explanation: Dividend paid is a financing outflow; AS-3 requires it to be disclosed separately.

revisionHistory.question: DIVIDEND PAID by a company is classified as:
options: FINANCING activity (it is a cost of obtaining financial resources)
revisionHistory.explanation: Dividend paid is a financing outflow; AS-3 requires it to be disclosed separately.

question: INTEREST and DIVIDENDS RECEIVED (non-financial enterprise) are:

options.text: Financing
INVESTING activities
Ignored
Operating

explanation: Returns on investments are investing inflows for non-financial enterprises.

question: The DIRECT method of reporting operating cash flows shows:

options.text: Only the net profit of the year, adjusted for nothing at all, as the single figure shown in it
MAJOR CLASSES of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments (cash from customers, cash paid to suppliers/employees etc.)
The profit adjusted only for the non-cash items
Only the changes in the balance sheet figures between the dates, with no direct listing of the receipts and the payments made

explanation: AS-3 encourages the direct method (gross receipts/payments); the indirect method starts from profit before tax and adjusts.

revisionHistory.question: The DIRECT method of reporting operating cash flows shows:
options: MAJOR CLASSES of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments (cash from customers, cash paid to suppliers/employees etc.)
revisionHistory.explanation: AS-3 encourages the direct method (gross receipts/payments); the indirect method starts from profit before tax and adjusts.

question: The INDIRECT method of computing cash flow from operations starts with:

options.text: The cash sales of the year, as the starting figure of the computation
The dividend paid during the year, as the starting figure of the computation
PROFIT BEFORE TAX and extraordinary items - adjusted for non-cash items (depreciation), non-operating items (interest), and changes in working capital

GROSS SALES of the year - adjusted for the cash sales, the credit sales, the returns inward, the trade discount allowed, the bad debts written off and the sales tax collected, every adjustment being made to arrive at the operating cash flow

explanation: Indirect method: PBT + depreciation +/- non-operating items +/- working-capital changes = cash from operations before tax.

revisionHistory.question: The INDIRECT method of computing cash flow from operations starts with:
options: PROFIT BEFORE TAX and extraordinary items - adjusted for non-cash items (depreciation), non-operating items (interest), and changes in working capital
revisionHistory.explanation: Indirect method: PBT + depreciation +/- non-operating items +/- working-capital changes = cash from operations before tax.

question: While computing operating cash flow (indirect method), an INCREASE in current assets is:

options.text: Ignored altogether in the computation, as a mere book figure
SUBTRACTED (an increase in debtors/stock means cash is tied up)
Added to the financing activities of the business, as an inflow
Added to the profit of the year, as an inflow of the cash

explanation: Increase in current assets = outflow; decrease = inflow. For current liabilities it is the reverse.

revisionHistory.question: While computing operating cash flow (indirect method), an INCREASE in current assets is:
options: SUBTRACTED (an increase in debtors/stock means cash is tied up)
revisionHistory.explanation: Increase in current assets = outflow; decrease = inflow. For current liabilities it is the reverse.

question: An INCREASE in current liabilities in the indirect method is:

options.text: An investing inflow of the business, shown on the investing side
Ignored altogether in the computation, as a mere book figure
ADDED to profit (higher creditors mean less cash paid out)
Subtracted from the profit of the year, as an outflow of the cash

explanation: Increase in current liabilities = cash conserved = added; decrease = subtracted.

revisionHistory.question: An INCREASE in current liabilities in the indirect method is:
options: ADDED to profit (higher creditors mean less cash paid out)
revisionHistory.explanation: Increase in current liabilities = cash conserved = added; decrease = subtracted.

question: Depreciation on machinery is dealt with in the indirect method by:

options.text: Subtracting it from the profit of the year, as an expense
ADDING it back to profit (a non-cash expense)
Ignoring it altogether in the computation, as a book entry
Showing it as a financing activity of the business, as an outflow

explanation: Depreciation, amortisation and provisions are non-cash charges added back to profit.

revisionHistory.question: Depreciation on machinery is dealt with in the indirect method by:
options: ADDING it back to profit (a non-cash expense)
revisionHistory.explanation: Depreciation, amortisation and provisions are non-cash charges added back to profit.

question: The purchase of a MACHINE by issuing DEBENTURES is:

options.text: A financing inflow of the business, since the debentures are issued
An operating outflow of the business, since the machine is bought
A NON-CASH transaction - EXCLUDED from the cash flow statement
An investing outflow of the business, since the machine is bought

explanation: Transactions not involving cash or cash equivalents are excluded from the cash flow statement (disclosed elsewhere).

revisionHistory.question: The purchase of a MACHINE by issuing DEBENTURES is:
options: A NON-CASH transaction - EXCLUDED from the cash flow statement
revisionHistory.explanation: Transactions not involving cash or cash equivalents are excluded from the cash flow statement (disclosed elsewhere).

question: A company reports profit before tax Rs.5,00,000, depreciation Rs.80,000, interest paid Rs.40,000 (financing), increase in debtors Rs.30,000, decrease in creditors Rs.20,000. Cash flow from OPERATIONS (before tax) is:
In the above question (tax paid Rs.1,00,000), NET cash from operating activities is:
Cash flow from INVESTING activities includes:

options.text: The payment of the interest on the loans of the business, year by year, as an investing flow always
PURCHASE and sale of fixed assets, investments, intangibles; interest and dividends received; loans advanced and recovered
The issue of the shares of the company to the public, for cash, as an investing flow always
The payment of the dividend to the shareholders of the company, year by year, as an investing flow

explanation: Investing covers acquisition/disposal of long-term assets and non-cash-equivalent investments.

revisionHistory.question: Cash flow from INVESTING activities includes:
options: PURCHASE and sale of fixed assets, investments, intangibles; interest and dividends received; loans advanced and recovered
revisionHistory.explanation: Investing covers acquisition/disposal of long-term assets and non-cash-equivalent investments.

question: Cash flow from FINANCING activities includes:

options.text: The sale of the patents of the business, for cash, during the year, as a financing flow always
PROCEEDS from issue of shares/debentures, long-term borrowings, their repayment, interest and dividends paid
The tax paid by the business during the year, in cash, as a financing flow always
The purchase of the goodwill of another business, for cash, as a financing flow always

explanation: Financing covers raising and servicing of capital - equity and debt.

revisionHistory.question: Cash flow from FINANCING activities includes:
options: PROCEEDS from issue of shares/debentures, long-term borrowings, their repayment, interest and dividends paid
revisionHistory.explanation: Financing covers raising and servicing of capital - equity and debt.

question: AS-3 (Cash Flow Statements) is applicable/mandatory to:

options.text: Only the banks of the country, and no other enterprise at all, whatever the size or the listing
Level I enterprises (listed/turnover above Rs.50 crore/borrowings above Rs.10 crore etc.); others are encouraged - companies must give it under the Companies Act via AS rules

Only the enterprises whose turnover is below one crore and whose borrowings are below one lakh - the smallest of the small - while every listed company and every large enterprise is wholly exempt from AS-3, whatever its size, its listing or its borrowings
Only the government companies of the country, and no other enterprise at all, whatever the size

explanation: AS-3 is mandatory for Level-I enterprises; for companies, the cash flow statement is part of financial statements where AS-3 applies.

revisionHistory.question: AS-3 (Cash Flow Statements) is applicable/mandatory to:
options: Level I enterprises (listed/turnover above Rs.50 crore/borrowings above Rs.10 crore etc.); others are encouraged - companies must give it under the Companies Act via AS rules
revisionHistory.explanation: AS-3 is mandatory for Level-I enterprises; for companies, the cash flow statement is part of financial statements where AS-3 applies.

question: A BANK (financial enterprise) reports interest received and paid under:

options.text: Investing
Cash equivalents
Financing
OPERATING activities

explanation: For financial enterprises, interest and dividends relating to their main business are operating cash flows.

question: The net increase in cash and cash equivalents shown by the cash flow statement equals:

options.text: The funds from the operations of the business, computed in the usual way
The difference between the OPENING and CLOSING balances of cash and cash equivalents
The change in the working capital of the business between the two dates
The net profit of the business for the year, after all adjustments

explanation: The three activity totals net to the movement in cash and equivalents, reconciling with the balance-sheet figures.

revisionHistory.question: The net increase in cash and cash equivalents shown by the cash flow statement equals:
options: The difference between the OPENING and CLOSING balances of cash and cash equivalents
revisionHistory.explanation: The three activity totals net to the movement in cash and equivalents, reconciling with the balance-sheet figures.

question: Foreign currency cash flows are recorded at:

options.text: The forward exchange rate fixed under the contract, even where the actual conversion takes place at a different spot rate on the date of the flow
The exchange rate on the DATE of the cash flow (or an average approximating it); unrealised exchange differences are NOT cash flows
The closing rate of the exchange always, whatever the date of the cash flow itself may be in the year
The historical rate of the exchange, at the date of the original transaction of the business itself always

explanation: AS-3/AS-11: use transaction-date rates; unrealised gains/losses from retranslation are not cash flows.

revisionHistory.question: Foreign currency cash flows are recorded at:
options: The exchange rate on the DATE of the cash flow (or an average approximating it); unrealised exchange differences are NOT cash flows
revisionHistory.explanation: AS-3/AS-11: use transaction-date rates; unrealised gains/losses from retranslation are not cash flows.

question: Cash flows from FUTURES, forwards, options and swaps are generally classified as:

options.text: OPERATING, unless they hedge identifiable investing or financing positions (then they follow the hedged item)
Investing always, whatever the position hedged by the contract of the business itself
Excluded from the statement altogether, as a derivative flow of the business itself
Financing always, whatever the position hedged by the contract of the business itself

explanation: Hedging instrument cash flows are classified the same way as the cash flows of the position being hedged.

revisionHistory.question: Cash flows from FUTURES, forwards, options and swaps are generally classified as:
options: OPERATING, unless they hedge identifiable investing or financing positions (then they follow the hedged item)
revisionHistory.explanation: Hedging instrument cash flows are classified the same way as the cash flows of the position being hedged.

question: Which of the following is a non-cash INVESTING AND FINANCING transaction excluded from the cash flow statement?

options.text: The interest paid on the borrowings of the business, during the year
The sale of the machinery of the business, for cash, during the year
Conversion of DEBENTURES into EQUITY SHARES
The dividend received on the investments of the business, during the year

explanation: Conversion of debt into equity moves no cash; such significant non-cash transactions are disclosed outside the statement.

revisionHistory.question: Which of the following is a non-cash INVESTING AND FINANCING transaction excluded from the cash flow statement?
options: Conversion of DEBENTURES into EQUITY SHARES
revisionHistory.explanation: Conversion of debt into equity moves no cash; such significant non-cash transactions are disclosed outside the statement.

question: An OVERDRAFT repayable on demand, forming an integral part of cash management, is:

options.text: INCLUDED as a component of cash and cash equivalents (negative component)
An investing item of the business, shown on the investing side
Ignored altogether in the statement, as a mere book figure
A financing inflow of the business, shown on the financing side

explanation: Bank overdrafts of this type reduce cash equivalents rather than appearing as financing flows.

revisionHistory.question: An OVERDRAFT repayable on demand, forming an integral part of cash management, is:
options: INCLUDED as a component of cash and cash equivalents (negative component)
revisionHistory.explanation: Bank overdrafts of this type reduce cash equivalents rather than appearing as financing flows.

question: The primary DIFFERENCE between a fund flow statement and a cash flow statement is:

options.text: FUND flow explains changes in WORKING CAPITAL; CASH flow explains changes in CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS only
No difference at all - the two statements are the same in every respect whatever
The cash flow statement is optional, while the fund flow statement is mandatory for all
The fund flow statement is audited, while the cash flow statement is never audited

explanation: Cash flow is narrower (cash basis, three activities) and is the statutorily prescribed one; fund flow works on the working-capital concept.

revisionHistory.question: The primary DIFFERENCE between a fund flow statement and a cash flow statement is:
options: FUND flow explains changes in WORKING CAPITAL; CASH flow explains changes in CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS only
revisionHistory.explanation: Cash flow is narrower (cash basis, three activities) and is the statutorily prescribed one; fund flow works on the working-capital concept.

question: While preparing a cash flow statement, an increase in the provision for doubtful debts (treated as a non-cash appropriation) is:

options.text: Subtracted from the profit in the operating activities, as an expense
A financing item of the business, shown on the financing side
Added back to profit in operating activities
An investing item of the business, shown on the investing side

explanation: Being a non-cash charge, the increase is added back (under the alternative treatment it may be deducted from debtors as a current-liability-style adjustment).

revisionHistory.question: While preparing a cash flow statement, an increase in the provision for doubtful debts (treated as a non-cash appropriation) is:
options: Added back to profit in operating activities
revisionHistory.explanation: Being a non-cash charge, the increase is added back (under the alternative treatment it may be deducted from debtors as a current-liability-style adjustment).

question: Cash GENERATED from operations is best described as:

options.text: The net profit shown in the profit and loss statement of the year, with no adjustment for the non-cash items or the working capital changes
The sales of the year less the purchases of the year
Operating profit BEFORE working-capital changes, adjusted for the working-capital changes - i.e. cash actually produced by operations
The EBITDA of the year only, before any working-capital adjustment at all is made in the year itself

explanation: It is the intermediate figure in the indirect method after adjusting profit for non-cash/non-operating items and working-capital movements, before deducting tax.

revisionHistory.question: Cash GENERATED from operations is best described as:
options: Operating profit BEFORE working-capital changes, adjusted for the working-capital changes - i.e. cash actually produced by operations
revisionHistory.explanation: It is the intermediate figure in the indirect method after adjusting profit for non-cash/non-operating items and working-capital movements, before deducting tax.

question: Capital budgeting is the process of:

options.text: Evaluating and selecting LONG-TERM INVESTMENT proposals whose returns flow over several years
The preparation of the annual budgets of the business, year after year, as a routine
The valuation of the goodwill of the business, from time to time, as required
The estimation of the daily cash requirements of the business, day after day

explanation: Capital budgeting commits funds to long-lived assets; decisions are hard to reverse and shape the firm future.

revisionHistory.question: Capital budgeting is the process of:

revisionHistory.explanation: Capital budgeting commits funds to long-lived assets; decisions are hard to reverse and shape the firm future.

question: Capital budgeting decisions are important because they involve:

options.text: Only the revenue expenses of the year, which are small and recurring in nature
The daily operations of the business, which are routine and repetitive in nature
LARGE, LONG-TERM, largely IRREVERSIBLE commitments that determine profitability and risk for years
Only the small sums of money, which are easily reversible at the will of the management

explanation: Size, longevity, irreversibility, risk and their effect on profitability make these the most critical financial decisions.

question: Which of the following is a NON-DISCOUNTING (traditional) technique of capital budgeting?

options.text: The IRR of the project, as the traditional measure
PAYBACK PERIOD and Accounting (Average) Rate of Return
The NPV of the project, as the traditional measure
The profitability index of the project, as the traditional measure

explanation: Payback and ARR ignore the time value of money; NPV, IRR and PI are discounted-cash-flow techniques.

revisionHistory.question: Which of the following is a NON-DISCOUNTING (traditional) technique of capital budgeting?
options: PAYBACK PERIOD and Accounting (Average) Rate of Return
revisionHistory.explanation: Payback and ARR ignore the time value of money; NPV, IRR and PI are discounted-cash-flow techniques.

question: The PAYBACK PERIOD is:

options.text: The life of the asset in years, as estimated by the management
The depreciation period of the asset, as fixed by the statute
The tenure of the loan taken for the asset, as fixed by the lender
The TIME REQUIRED TO RECOVER the initial cash outlay from the annual cash inflows

explanation: Payback = initial investment / annual cash inflow (for even inflows); shorter is better.

revisionHistory.question: The PAYBACK PERIOD is:
options: The TIME REQUIRED TO RECOVER the initial cash outlay from the annual cash inflows
revisionHistory.explanation: Payback = initial investment / annual cash inflow (for even inflows); shorter is better.

question: A machine costs Rs.5,00,000 and generates even annual cash inflows of Rs.1,00,000. Its payback period is:

options.text: 4 years
6 years
10 years
5 years

question: For UNEVEN cash inflows, the payback period is found by:

options.text: Using the IRR of the project, with the usual tables of the present value
CUMULATING the annual inflows until they equal the outlay (interpolation for the part-year)
Dividing the cost of the project by the average inflow of the years of its life
Using the ARR of the project, with the usual formula of the average profit

explanation: Cumulative inflows: payback = completed years + (unrecovered amount / inflow of the next year).

revisionHistory.question: For UNEVEN cash inflows, the payback period is found by:
options: CUMULATING the annual inflows until they equal the outlay (interpolation for the part-year)
revisionHistory.explanation: Cumulative inflows: payback = completed years + (unrecovered amount / inflow of the next year).

question: A project costs Rs.2,00,000 with inflows: Y1 Rs.80,000, Y2 Rs.60,000, Y3 Rs.50,000, Y4 Rs.40,000. Payback period is:
