4 years
3 years
3.25 years

question: The MAIN merit of the payback method is:

options.text: It maximises the wealth of the shareholders by choosing the most profitable project out of all the proposals every time
It considers the time value of the money, in every computation of the payback
It considers the total profitability of the project, over its whole life of years
Its SIMPLICITY and its stress on LIQUIDITY/early recovery - suited to risky, fast-obsolescing investments

explanation: Payback is easy to compute and favours quick-recovery projects; that is why overleveraged or risk-averse firms use it.

revisionHistory.question: The MAIN merit of the payback method is:
options: Its SIMPLICITY and its stress on LIQUIDITY/early recovery - suited to risky, fast-obsolescing investments
revisionHistory.explanation: Payback is easy to compute and favours quick-recovery projects; that is why overleveraged or risk-averse firms use it.

question: The DEMERITS of the payback method include:

options.text: It uses the discounted flows of the project, in every computation of the period
It requires a cut-off rate of return, fixed by the management of the company
It IGNORES the time value of money AND cash flows AFTER the payback period (total profitability)
It is too complex for the ordinary manager to apply in the practice of the business

explanation: Payback ignores both discounting and post-payback returns - a project with high later inflows may be wrongly rejected.

revisionHistory.question: The DEMERITS of the payback method include:
options: It IGNORES the time value of money AND cash flows AFTER the payback period (total profitability)
revisionHistory.explanation: Payback ignores both discounting and post-payback returns - a project with high later inflows may be wrongly rejected.

question: POST-PAYBACK profitability is:

options.text: The total investment made in the project, at the start
The profit/cash inflows earned AFTER the initial investment has been recovered
The profit earned within the payback period itself, and nothing beyond it at all
The scrap value of the asset, at the end of its life

explanation: Post-payback profitability = total inflows - initial outlay (the surplus earned beyond recovery).

revisionHistory.question: POST-PAYBACK profitability is:
options: The profit/cash inflows earned AFTER the initial investment has been recovered
revisionHistory.explanation: Post-payback profitability = total inflows - initial outlay (the surplus earned beyond recovery).

question: The DISCOUNTED payback period improves on simple payback by:

options.text: Ignoring the scrap value of the asset, at the end of its life
Using the book profit of the project, instead of the cash flows
Discounting the cash inflows BEFORE computing the recovery period
Ignoring the time value of the money, in every computation

explanation: Discounted payback applies the time value of money to inflows but still ignores flows beyond recovery.

revisionHistory.question: The DISCOUNTED payback period improves on simple payback by:
options: Discounting the cash inflows BEFORE computing the recovery period
revisionHistory.explanation: Discounted payback applies the time value of money to inflows but still ignores flows beyond recovery.

question: The ACCOUNTING (Average) RATE OF RETURN (ARR) is:

options.text: The investment of the project divided by the profit of the year, times 100
AVERAGE ANNUAL PROFIT (after depreciation and tax) / AVERAGE (or initial) INVESTMENT x 100
The NPV of the project divided by the investment of the project, times 100
The annual cash inflow divided by the investment of the project, times 100

explanation: ARR is a profit-based, non-discounted measure; projects are accepted if ARR exceeds the target rate.

revisionHistory.question: The ACCOUNTING (Average) RATE OF RETURN (ARR) is:
options: AVERAGE ANNUAL PROFIT (after depreciation and tax) / AVERAGE (or initial) INVESTMENT x 100
revisionHistory.explanation: ARR is a profit-based, non-discounted measure; projects are accepted if ARR exceeds the target rate.

question: A project needs an investment of Rs.5,00,000 (no scrap value) and yields average annual accounting profit of Rs.60,000. ARR on AVERAGE investment is:
explanation: Average investment = (5,00,000 + 0)/2 = 2,50,000; ARR = 60,000/2,50,000 = 24% (on initial investment it is 12%).

question: In capital budgeting, the relevant cash flows are:

options.text: The gross margins of the project, year by year, before any expense of the business at all
The accounting profits of the project, year by year, as per the books of the business itself
The sales figures of the project, year by year, as per the estimates of the management alone
INCREMENTAL after-tax CASH flows (profit after tax + depreciation), ignoring sunk costs and allocated overheads

explanation: Decisions use incremental cash flows; depreciation is added back (non-cash) though its tax shield matters; sunk costs are irrelevant.

revisionHistory.question: In capital budgeting, the relevant cash flows are:
options: INCREMENTAL after-tax CASH flows (profit after tax + depreciation), ignoring sunk costs and allocated overheads
revisionHistory.explanation: Decisions use incremental cash flows; depreciation is added back (non-cash) though its tax shield matters; sunk costs are irrelevant.

question: Depreciation enters capital budgeting cash-flow computation because:

options.text: It is a cash cost of the year, paid out in money every year by the business itself
It has no bearing on the decision at all, being a fixed charge of the year always
It is a NON-CASH expense that SAVES TAX - cash inflow = PAT + depreciation (or EBIT(1-t) + depreciation)
It increases the cash of the business, being an inflow of the year of its own charge

explanation: Depreciation itself is not a cash flow, but it shields taxable profit; the standard conversion adds it back to PAT.

revisionHistory.question: Depreciation enters capital budgeting cash-flow computation because:
options: It is a NON-CASH expense that SAVES TAX - cash inflow = PAT + depreciation (or EBIT(1-t) + depreciation)
revisionHistory.explanation: Depreciation itself is not a cash flow, but it shields taxable profit; the standard conversion adds it back to PAT.

question: A SUNK cost in capital budgeting is:

options.text: A cost ALREADY INCURRED that cannot be recovered - IRRELEVANT to the accept/reject decision
A working-capital need of the project, recurring every year of its useful life
The salvage value of the asset, at the end of its own useful life
A future cost of the project, yet to be incurred by the business itself

explanation: Only future incremental flows matter; sunk costs (e.g. research already done) do not change with the decision.

revisionHistory.question: A SUNK cost in capital budgeting is:
options: A cost ALREADY INCURRED that cannot be recovered - IRRELEVANT to the accept/reject decision
revisionHistory.explanation: Only future incremental flows matter; sunk costs (e.g. research already done) do not change with the decision.

question: The initial investment in a project includes:

options.text: Only the cost of installing the asset
Cost of the asset + installation + working capital margin, net of any sale proceeds of the replaced asset
Only the equity-financed portion of the cost of the asset
Only the purchase price of the asset itself

explanation: The outlay is the full incremental commitment: asset cost, erection/installation, additional working capital, less realisations from the old asset.

revisionHistory.question: The initial investment in a project includes:
options: Cost of the asset + installation + working capital margin, net of any sale proceeds of the replaced asset

question: Terminal cash flows of a project include:

options.text: SALVAGE value (net of tax) and RECOVERY of working capital at the end of the project life
The interest paid on the borrowings of the project, at the end of its life
The initial cost of the asset, recovered at the end of the life
The annual depreciation of the asset, at the end of the life of the project

explanation: The final year adds scrap/salvage proceeds and release of working capital to the operating inflow.

revisionHistory.question: Terminal cash flows of a project include:
options: SALVAGE value (net of tax) and RECOVERY of working capital at the end of the project life

question: The accept rule under the payback method is:

options.text: Accept the project if its payback equals its ARR
ACCEPT if the payback period is LESS than the maximum acceptable period set by management
Accept every project whatever its payback period
Accept the project if its payback exceeds the life of the asset in the appraisal made by it

explanation: Compare the computed payback with the predetermined cut-off; among mutually exclusive projects, the shortest payback wins.

revisionHistory.question: The accept rule under the payback method is:
options: ACCEPT if the payback period is LESS than the maximum acceptable period set by management
revisionHistory.explanation: Compare the computed payback with the predetermined cut-off; among mutually exclusive projects, the shortest payback wins.

question: The accept rule under ARR is:

options.text: ARR equal to zero
ARR equal to the IRR of the project under evaluation by it
ARR below the cost of capital
ARR ABOVE the minimum/target rate fixed by management

explanation: Projects meeting the target accounting return are accepted; mutually exclusive choices pick the highest ARR.

revisionHistory.question: The accept rule under ARR is:
options: ARR ABOVE the minimum/target rate fixed by management
revisionHistory.explanation: Projects meeting the target accounting return are accepted; mutually exclusive choices pick the highest ARR.

question: In MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE projects, choosing one project:

options.text: Doubles the returns expected from the chosen project over the whole of its life
AUTOMATICALLY REJECTS the alternatives (they compete for the same purpose)
Leaves the other alternatives wholly unaffected
Permits the other alternatives to be chosen as well

explanation: Mutually exclusive projects serve the same need; independent projects can all be accepted if they clear the hurdle.

revisionHistory.question: In MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE projects, choosing one project:

question: Capital RATIONING exists when:

options.text: The payback of every project is short, so that the funds of the firm suffice for all of them at once, whatever the size
The firm has MORE acceptable projects than it can finance with the available capital - projects must be ranked and combined within the budget
The IRR of every project is negative, so that none of them can be taken up at all by the firm ever, whatever
The funds of the firm are unlimited, so that every acceptable project can be taken up at once by it, whatever

explanation: Under capital rationing, select the combination of projects that maximises total NPV within the budget constraint.

revisionHistory.question: Capital RATIONING exists when:

revisionHistory.explanation: Under capital rationing, select the combination of projects that maximises total NPV within the budget constraint.

question: Risk analysis in capital budgeting does NOT use:

options.text: Sensitivity analysis
Scenario/simulation analysis
CERTAINTY of cash flows assumption
Standard deviation and coefficient of variation

explanation: Risk techniques (sensitivity, SD/CV, risk-adjusted rate, certainty equivalents, decision trees, simulation) exist precisely because flows are uncertain.

question: The RISK-ADJUSTED DISCOUNT RATE approach handles risk by:

options.text: Adding a RISK PREMIUM to the risk-free rate for discounting project flows
Ignoring the risk of the project altogether, in the computation
Reducing the cash flows of the project to zero, in the computation
Using the payback of the project, as the only measure of the risk

explanation: Riskier projects are discounted at higher rates; the certainty-equivalent approach instead scales down the flows themselves.

options.text: COST-BENEFIT ANALYSIS (including social costs and benefits)
The ARR of the project, as the usual measure
The book value of the assets, as the usual measure
The payback of the project only, as the usual measure

options.text: Money to be received in future is worth more than money in hand today for the firm
The money loses its value only due to the inflation, and for no other reason
The value of the money never changes at all, whatever the time
A rupee TODAY is worth MORE than a rupee tomorrow because of its earning potential

explanation: Money can earn interest; receiving earlier allows reinvestment. Discounting (present value) and compounding (future value) are opposite processes.

options.text: Annuity; perpetuity

Future value; present value
IRR; NPV

explanation: Discounting converts future flows to today value at the required rate; compounding carries present sums forward.

An annuity due
An annuity
Future value

options.text: Irregularly
At the END of each period
Only once
At the BEGINNING of each period

explanation: Annuity-due payments fall at period starts (like rent/lease in advance), making each payment discount one period less.

question: NET PRESENT VALUE (NPV) is:

options.text: The PRESENT VALUE of future cash inflows MINUS the present value of cash outflows (initial investment)
The total inflows of the project minus the total outflows, without any discounting at all
The IRR of the project minus the cost of the capital of the firm, as computed
The profit of the year less the tax of the year, computed after charging all expenses of every kind, cash or otherwise

explanation: NPV discounts all flows at the cost of capital; it measures the net addition to wealth in absolute rupees.

options.text: Accept the project if its NPV is negative
Accept every project whatever its NPV
Accept if NPV is POSITIVE (> 0); reject if negative; indifferent at zero
Accept the project only if its NPV is exactly zero at the appraisal stage

question: If the NPV of a project is ZERO, it means:

options.text: The IRR of the project works out to zero
The project earns EXACTLY the required rate of return (the discount rate) - it recovers the investment plus the required return
The project runs at a loss throughout its life
The project yields no cash inflows at all

explanation: Zero NPV = inflows discounted at the required rate exactly cover the outlay; the firm is indifferent.

revisionHistory.question: If the NPV of a project is ZERO, it means:

question: The INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR) is the discount rate at which:

options.text: The ARR of the project equals the cost of the capital, at that rate
NPV EQUALS ZERO (PV of inflows = PV of outflows)
The payback of the project is the shortest possible, at that rate
The NPV of the project is the maximum possible, at that rate

explanation: IRR is the break-even discount rate; it is found by trial and error/interpolation between two rates with opposite-sign NPVs.

Both of them ignore the time value of the money, in every computation of the conflict whatever it may be at all
The rates of tax applicable to the firm over the years, which change the discount rate and hence push the two methods in opposite directions each time
DIFFERENCES IN PROJECT SIZE (investment disparity) or in the TIMING/PATTERN of cash flows (and unconventional flows causing multiple IRRs)

question: When NPV and IRR conflict for MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE projects, the decision should follow:

options.text: The payback of the projects, as the better measure of the wealth of the shareholders
The ARR of the projects, as the better measure of the wealth of the shareholders

The IRR of the projects, as the better measure of the wealth of the shareholders

The IRR of the project under evaluation by the firm

Decide first, then discount, compute, and identify the rate, in that order

It is EASY to compute and needs no discount rate
It considers ALL cash flows over the project life
It recognises the time value of money

Ignoring the time value of the money, in every computation of the modified rate
Leaving out the discount rate from the computation of the terminal value of the project entirely
Using the book profits of the project, instead of the cash flows of the project

revisionHistory.explanation: MIRR compounds positive flows at the finance/reinvestment rate to the end, then finds the single rate equating them to the PV of outflows - one unique answer.

The share capital of the firm, as subscribed by the shareholders of the company
The total assets of the firm, at their balance-sheet values as on the date
The book profit of the firm, as per its accounts of the year under review

explanation: Wealth maximisation discounts the entire expected benefit stream; it is the theoretically correct goal of financial management.

options.text: IGNORES timing (time value), risk, quality of benefits and is VAGUE about which profit (short/long run, before/after tax)
It adds directly to the wealth of the shareholders
It takes full account of the risks of the business
It is too precise about the profit to be pursued

explanation: Profit maximisation is ambiguous, ignores time value and risk, and can invite short-sighted decisions; wealth maximisation answers all three.

The unlimited funds, where every project can be taken

Avoid the computation altogether, by a simple guess of the management of it
Fix the discount rate of the project, once for all its years of life
Model the PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION of NPV/IRR by repeatedly sampling uncertain variables

question: CERTAINTY EQUIVALENT approach adjusts:

options.text: The discount rate, multiplied by a certainty coefficient
The payback period, multiplied by a certainty coefficient
The CASH FLOWS - uncertain flows are multiplied by certainty-equivalent coefficients, then discounted at the RISK-FREE rate
The tax rates, multiplied by a certainty coefficient

explanation: Certainty equivalents convert risky flows into their sure equivalents, discounted at the risk-free rate - the risk adjustment sits in the numerator.

revisionHistory.question: CERTAINTY EQUIVALENT approach adjusts:
options: The CASH FLOWS - uncertain flows are multiplied by certainty-equivalent coefficients, then discounted at the RISK-FREE rate
revisionHistory.explanation: Certainty equivalents convert risky flows into their sure equivalents, discounted at the risk-free rate - the risk adjustment sits in the numerator.

question: Cost of capital is:

options.text: The coupon rate on the debt of the firm, as fixed in the debenture trust deed at the time of the issue of the debentures
The bank rate of the RBI, as announced by the central bank from time to time in its credit policy statements
The MINIMUM RATE OF RETURN a firm must earn on its investments to keep the market value of its shares unchanged (the opportunity cost of funds)
The dividend rate of the firm, as declared by the board of directors at the annual general meeting of the year

explanation: Cost of capital is the cut-off/hurdle rate for investment decisions and the discount rate in NPV.

revisionHistory.question: Cost of capital is:
options: The MINIMUM RATE OF RETURN a firm must earn on its investments to keep the market value of its shares unchanged (the opportunity cost of funds)
revisionHistory.explanation: Cost of capital is the cut-off/hurdle rate for investment decisions and the discount rate in NPV.

question: The cost of capital is used in financial management mainly for:

options.text: ACCEPT-REJECT decisions in capital budgeting (discount/hurdle rate) and designing the optimal capital structure
The audit of the accounts of the firm, as required by the statute for every company registered under the Act
The preparation of the budgets of the firm, year after year, as a routine exercise of the management
The filing of the tax returns of the firm, year after year, as required by the Income-tax Act

explanation: It links investment and financing decisions: projects must clear it, and the mix of funds should minimise it.

revisionHistory.question: The cost of capital is used in financial management mainly for:
options: ACCEPT-REJECT decisions in capital budgeting (discount/hurdle rate) and designing the optimal capital structure
revisionHistory.explanation: It links investment and financing decisions: projects must clear it, and the mix of funds should minimise it.

question: The cost of DEBT (Kd) is computed on a(n) ________ basis:

options.text: The accrual basis only, whatever the tax position of the firm
The pre-tax basis, since the interest is paid before the tax
AFTER-TAX basis: Kd = I(1 - t)/NP because interest is TAX-DEDUCTIBLE
The gross basis, without any adjustment for the tax at all

explanation: Interest tax shield: effective cost = interest x (1 - tax rate) divided by net proceeds of the debenture.

revisionHistory.question: The cost of DEBT (Kd) is computed on a(n) ________ basis:
options: AFTER-TAX basis: Kd = I(1 - t)/NP because interest is TAX-DEDUCTIBLE
revisionHistory.explanation: Interest tax shield: effective cost = interest x (1 - tax rate) divided by net proceeds of the debenture.

question: A company issues 10% debentures of Rs.100 at par; tax rate 30%. The after-tax cost of debt is:
A 12% debenture of Rs.100 is issued at a PREMIUM of 10% (net proceeds Rs.110); tax 40%. Approximate cost of debt is:
The cost of PREFERENCE capital (Kp) is:

options.text: The interest of the year divided by the net proceeds of the issue of the debentures, as computed
The preference dividend multiplied by (1 minus the tax rate), divided by the net proceeds of the issue
The preference dividend divided by the face value of the shares, with full tax adjustment for the dividend paid
PREFERENCE DIVIDEND / NET PROCEEDS - NO tax adjustment, since preference dividend is NOT a deductible expense

explanation: Preference dividend is an appropriation, not a charge; hence no (1-t) factor.

revisionHistory.question: The cost of PREFERENCE capital (Kp) is:
options: PREFERENCE DIVIDEND / NET PROCEEDS - NO tax adjustment, since preference dividend is NOT a deductible expense
revisionHistory.explanation: Preference dividend is an appropriation, not a charge; hence no (1-t) factor.

question: A company issues 8% preference shares of Rs.100 at par. Cost of preference capital is:
explanation: Kp = 8/100 = 8% (no tax adjustment).

question: The cost of EQUITY share capital (Ke) under the DIVIDEND PRICE approach is:

options.text: The dividend of the year divided by the face value of the share
Dividend per share / MARKET PRICE per share (Ke = D/P0)
The EPS of the year divided by the market price of the share
Dividend per share divided by the book value per share

explanation: Ke = D1/P0 under constant dividend; with constant growth g, the Gordon form is Ke = D1/P0 + g.

revisionHistory.question: The cost of EQUITY share capital (Ke) under the DIVIDEND PRICE approach is:
options: Dividend per share / MARKET PRICE per share (Ke = D/P0)
revisionHistory.explanation: Ke = D1/P0 under constant dividend; with constant growth g, the Gordon form is Ke = D1/P0 + g.

question: Under the DIVIDEND PRICE PLUS GROWTH (Gordon) model, Ke =

options.text: D1/P0 + G (dividend yield plus the constant growth rate)
The dividend multiplied by (1 minus the tax rate), divided by the price
The dividend divided by the price, with no growth at all
The EPS divided by the price, plus the growth rate of the firm

explanation: The constant-growth model adds the expected perpetual dividend growth rate to the forward dividend yield.

revisionHistory.question: Under the DIVIDEND PRICE PLUS GROWTH (Gordon) model, Ke =
options: D1/P0 + G (dividend yield plus the constant growth rate)
revisionHistory.explanation: The constant-growth model adds the expected perpetual dividend growth rate to the forward dividend yield.

question: A share sells at Rs.50; expected dividend next year Rs.5, growing at 6% forever. Ke is:
The EARNINGS-PRICE approach estimates Ke as:

options.text: Market price per share divided by the EPS
Book value per share divided by the market price of the share in the stock market
EPS / MARKET PRICE (appropriate when earnings are fully distributed or stable)
Dividend per share divided by the market price

explanation: Ke = EPS/P0; it approximates the capitalisation rate of a no-growth, full-payout firm.

revisionHistory.question: The EARNINGS-PRICE approach estimates Ke as:
options: EPS / MARKET PRICE (appropriate when earnings are fully distributed or stable)
revisionHistory.explanation: Ke = EPS/P0; it approximates the capitalisation rate of a no-growth, full-payout firm.

question: The cost of RETAINED EARNINGS (Kr) is:

options.text: EQUAL to the cost of equity (opportunity cost of dividends forgone), sometimes adjusted for personal tax and flotation saved
Zero always - the retained earnings are free funds of the firm, with no cost at all attached to them whatever
Half of the cost of the equity capital
Equal to the cost of the debt of the firm, since retained earnings carry the same safety and the same claim as the borrowings do

explanation: Retained earnings carry an opportunity cost equal to what shareholders could earn outside (Ke); no flotation cost is incurred.

revisionHistory.question: The cost of RETAINED EARNINGS (Kr) is:
options: EQUAL to the cost of equity (opportunity cost of dividends forgone), sometimes adjusted for personal tax and flotation saved
revisionHistory.explanation: Retained earnings carry an opportunity cost equal to what shareholders could earn outside (Ke); no flotation cost is incurred.

question: FLOTATION costs on a NEW equity issue:

options.text: Are ignored in computing the cost of the new equity raised by the company in the issue
INCREASE the effective cost - Ke = D1 / P0(1 - f) + g, because net proceeds fall
Reduce the Ke of the firm, since the issue becomes cheaper
Reduce the cost of the debt of the firm, since the issue becomes cheaper

explanation: Flotation cost reduces net proceeds, raising the cost of new equity above that of retained earnings.

revisionHistory.question: FLOTATION costs on a NEW equity issue:
options: INCREASE the effective cost - Ke = D1 / P0(1 - f) + g, because net proceeds fall
revisionHistory.explanation: Flotation cost reduces net proceeds, raising the cost of new equity above that of retained earnings.

question: The WEIGHTED AVERAGE COST OF CAPITAL (WACC / Ko) is:

options.text: The Ke of the firm always, whatever the structure of the capital of the firm may be in the year
The highest of the component costs in the structure, taken as the single rate the firm must pay for all of its funds
The simple average of the component costs, without any weights at all attached to the components
The SUM OF COMPONENT COSTS WEIGHTED BY their PROPORTIONS in the capital structure (book or market value weights)

explanation: Ko = sum of (weight x after-tax cost) for debt, preference, equity and retained earnings.

revisionHistory.question: The WEIGHTED AVERAGE COST OF CAPITAL (WACC / Ko) is:
options: The simple average of component costs
The SUM OF COMPONENT COSTS WEIGHTED BY their PROPORTIONS in the capital structure (book or market value weights)
revisionHistory.explanation: Ko = sum of (weight x after-tax cost) for debt, preference, equity and retained earnings.

question: A firm has equity (Rs.6,00,000, Ke 16%) and debt (Rs.4,00,000, after-tax Kd 8%). WACC is:
MARKET VALUE weights are preferred to book value weights in WACC because:

options.text: They reflect the CURRENT economic proportions in which investors value the firm
They are constant over the years, unlike the book values of the securities of the firm
They are easier to compute than the book values of the securities of the firm
Book value weights are not permitted by law for this purpose

explanation: Market values track the true opportunity costs; book weights can be badly outdated (though stable and always available).

revisionHistory.question: MARKET VALUE weights are preferred to book value weights in WACC because:
options: They reflect the CURRENT economic proportions in which investors value the firm
revisionHistory.explanation: Market values track the true opportunity costs; book weights can be badly outdated (though stable and always available).

question: The MARGINAL cost of capital is:

options.text: The cost of the debt portion of the firm's total capital raised
The cost of the ADDITIONAL (next) rupee of new capital raised
The historical cost of the capital of the firm, as recorded
The average of all the past capital raised by the firm

explanation: Marginal cost matters for new investment decisions; it may jump at break points where retained earnings are exhausted.

revisionHistory.question: The MARGINAL cost of capital is:
options: The cost of the ADDITIONAL (next) rupee of new capital raised
The average of all past capital
revisionHistory.explanation: Marginal cost matters for new investment decisions; it may jump at break points where retained earnings are exhausted.

question: A firm keeps its debt-equity at 40:60 and has Rs.3,00,000 of retained earnings (Ke 14%) before needing new equity (Ke 16%). The BREAK POINT for the equity component is:
explanation: Break point = retained earnings / equity weight = 3,00,000 / 0.60 = Rs.5,00,000 of total new financing.

question: The cost of capital for an ALL-EQUITY firm is:

options.text: Kp only
Kd only
Zero always, since the equity has no cost at all
Ke only (WACC = cost of equity)

explanation: With no debt or preference, the weighted average reduces to the cost of equity.

revisionHistory.question: The cost of capital for an ALL-EQUITY firm is:
revisionHistory.explanation: With no debt or preference, the weighted average reduces to the cost of equity.

question: Explicit cost of capital refers to:

options.text: Zero cost always, since the explicit sources of the capital are free to the firm
The rate the firm must PAY on the specific source (e.g. interest rate on debt)
The implied cost of the source, as computed by the analyst of the firm
The opportunity cost of the source, as computed by the analyst of the firm

explanation: Explicit cost is the contractual rate; implicit (opportunity) cost attaches to sources like retained earnings.

revisionHistory.question: Explicit cost of capital refers to:
options: The rate the firm must PAY on the specific source (e.g. interest rate on debt)
revisionHistory.explanation: Explicit cost is the contractual rate; implicit (opportunity) cost attaches to sources like retained earnings.

question: Redeemable debentures cost formula (approximation) is:

options.text: Interest for the year divided by the redeemable value
Dividend for the year divided by the price of the share
Kd = [I(1-t) + (RV - NP)/n] / [(RV + NP)/2], where RV = redeemable value, NP = net proceeds
Interest multiplied by (1 - tax rate), divided by the net proceeds of the debenture issue made

explanation: For redeemable debt, the amortisation of the redemption premium/discount over the life is added to the after-tax interest.

revisionHistory.question: Redeemable debentures cost formula (approximation) is:
options: Kd = [I(1-t) + (RV - NP)/n] / [(RV + NP)/2], where RV = redeemable value, NP = net proceeds
revisionHistory.explanation: For redeemable debt, the amortisation of the redemption premium/discount over the life is added to the after-tax interest.

question: CAPM estimates the cost of equity as:

options.text: EPS divided by the market price of the share
Dividend divided by the price, plus the growth rate of dividends expected in future
Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf) - risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium
Cost of debt plus the rate of tax

explanation: CAPM prices systematic risk only: Ke = Rf + beta(Rm - Rf).

revisionHistory.question: CAPM estimates the cost of equity as:
options: Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf) - risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium
revisionHistory.explanation: CAPM prices systematic risk only: Ke = Rf + beta(Rm - Rf).

question: A share has beta 1.4, risk-free rate 7%, expected market return 15%. Ke (CAPM) is:
Beta measures:

options.text: The unsystematic risk of the security, specific to the firm and its own affairs
The liquidity of the security, in the market where it is traded daily
SYSTEMATIC (market/non-diversifiable) risk of a security relative to the market
The total risk of the security, including every kind of risk whatever

explanation: Beta = covariance with market / market variance; beta > 1 means more volatile than the market.

revisionHistory.question: Beta measures:
options: SYSTEMATIC (market/non-diversifiable) risk of a security relative to the market
revisionHistory.explanation: Beta = covariance with market / market variance; beta > 1 means more volatile than the market.

question: As the proportion of CHEAP DEBT rises initially, the overall cost of capital (Ko) typically:

options.text: FALLS (up to a prudent limit), because cheaper after-tax debt replaces costly equity - beyond a point rising financial risk reverses it
Stays fixed at the same level, whatever the proportion of the debt in the structure of the capital of the firm may be
Becomes zero at once, as soon as the debt is introduced into the structure of the capital of the firm at all
Rises at once, as soon as the debt is introduced into the structure of the capital of the firm at all

explanation: Moderate leverage lowers WACC (the tax-shield benefit); excessive leverage raises both Ke and Kd, pushing WACC back up.

revisionHistory.question: As the proportion of CHEAP DEBT rises initially, the overall cost of capital (Ko) typically:
options: FALLS (up to a prudent limit), because cheaper after-tax debt replaces costly equity - beyond a point rising financial risk reverses it
revisionHistory.explanation: Moderate leverage lowers WACC (the tax-shield benefit); excessive leverage raises both Ke and Kd, pushing WACC back up.

question: CAPITAL STRUCTURE refers to:

options.text: The total assets of the firm, at their balance-sheet values as on the date of the accounts
The current liabilities of the firm, as on the date of the balance sheet of the year
The share capital of the firm taken by itself, apart from its debt and its reserves and surplus
The MIX/PROPORTION of LONG-TERM sources of funds - debt, preference and equity - used by a firm

explanation: Capital structure is the composition of long-term financing; the decision trades off cheaper debt against financial risk.

revisionHistory.question: CAPITAL STRUCTURE refers to:
options: The MIX/PROPORTION of LONG-TERM sources of funds - debt, preference and equity - used by a firm
revisionHistory.explanation: Capital structure is the composition of long-term financing; the decision trades off cheaper debt against financial risk.

question: The CAPITALISATION of a firm includes:

options.text: Only the long-term debt raised by the firm from the market, and not its share capital or reserves at all
ALL long-term securities issued plus reserves and surplus (the total long-term funds raised)
The current assets of the firm, at their balance-sheet values as on the date of accounts
Only the equity capital raised by the firm

explanation: Capitalisation = total long-term capital employed (share capital, reserves, long-term debt); capital structure is its composition.

revisionHistory.question: The CAPITALISATION of a firm includes:
options: ALL long-term securities issued plus reserves and surplus (the total long-term funds raised)
revisionHistory.explanation: Capitalisation = total long-term capital employed (share capital, reserves, long-term debt); capital structure is its composition.

question: An OPTIMAL capital structure is one that:

options.text: Ignores the risks of the business altogether and entirely in its working
Uses only debt in the financing mix
MAXIMISES the value of the firm / MINIMISES the overall cost of capital
Uses only equity in the financing mix

explanation: The optimum balances the tax-shield benefit of debt against rising bankruptcy/agency costs so that WACC is lowest and value highest.

revisionHistory.question: An OPTIMAL capital structure is one that:
options: MAXIMISES the value of the firm / MINIMISES the overall cost of capital
revisionHistory.explanation: The optimum balances the tax-shield benefit of debt against rising bankruptcy/agency costs so that WACC is lowest and value highest.

question: Under the NET INCOME (NI) approach (Durand), the value of the firm:

options.text: Independent of the degree of leverage employed
Always zero, irrespective of the leverage employed
Falls as the leverage of the firm rises
INCREASES with leverage - since debt is cheaper and Ke and Kd are assumed CONSTANT, WACC falls as debt rises

explanation: NI assumes constant Ke and Kd, so more cheap debt always lowers Ko; the optimum is (nearly) 100% debt.

revisionHistory.question: Under the NET INCOME (NI) approach (Durand), the value of the firm:
options: INCREASES with leverage - since debt is cheaper and Ke and Kd are assumed CONSTANT, WACC falls as debt rises
revisionHistory.explanation: NI assumes constant Ke and Kd, so more cheap debt always lowers Ko; the optimum is (nearly) 100% debt.

question: Under the NET OPERATING INCOME (NOI) approach, the value of the firm is:

options.text: Zero always, whatever the structure of the capital of the firm may be in the year of account
Decreased by the use of debt in the structure, since the lenders charge a heavy price for the risk they are asked to bear
Increased by the use of debt in the structure
INDEPENDENT of the capital structure - Ko stays constant because Ke rises exactly enough to offset cheaper debt

explanation: NOI holds that the market capitalises operating income at a constant Ko; leverage only shifts risk to equity (Ke rises), leaving V unchanged.

revisionHistory.question: Under the NET OPERATING INCOME (NOI) approach, the value of the firm is:
options: INDEPENDENT of the capital structure - Ko stays constant because Ke rises exactly enough to offset cheaper debt
revisionHistory.explanation: NOI holds that the market capitalises operating income at a constant Ko; leverage only shifts risk to equity (Ke rises), leaving V unchanged.

question: The TRADITIONAL approach to capital structure says:

options.text: Ko FIRST FALLS with moderate leverage, then RISES beyond a point - an OPTIMAL structure exists where Ko is minimum
The structure has no effect at all on the value of the firm, in any case whatever the level of debt
Debt should form the whole of the capital structure of the firm, equity being avoided altogether because of its heavy cost
The Ko of the firm is constant, whatever the leverage of the firm may be in the year of account

explanation: The traditional view is intermediate: moderate debt lowers Ko, but beyond a limit Ke (and Kd) rise sharply, so an optimum exists.

revisionHistory.question: The TRADITIONAL approach to capital structure says:
options: Ko FIRST FALLS with moderate leverage, then RISES beyond a point - an OPTIMAL structure exists where Ko is minimum
revisionHistory.explanation: The traditional view is intermediate: moderate debt lowers Ko, but beyond a limit Ke (and Kd) rise sharply, so an optimum exists.

question: Under the MODIGLIANI-MILLER (MM) hypothesis WITHOUT taxes, the value of the firm:

options.text: Increases as the debt of the firm rises
Decreases as the debt of the firm rises
Equals the value of the debt of the firm
Is INDEPENDENT of capital structure (value depends on operating income and business risk only); ARBITRAGE enforces this

explanation: MM-no-tax: identical firms must have identical total value regardless of leverage; homemade leverage/arbitrage drives them together.

revisionHistory.question: Under the MODIGLIANI-MILLER (MM) hypothesis WITHOUT taxes, the value of the firm:
options: Is INDEPENDENT of capital structure (value depends on operating income and business risk only); ARBITRAGE enforces this
revisionHistory.explanation: MM-no-tax: identical firms must have identical total value regardless of leverage; homemade leverage/arbitrage drives them together.

question: Under MM WITH corporate taxes, the value of a LEVERED firm is:

options.text: Zero always, since the tax shield does not exist at all for the firm
VALUE OF UNLEVERED FIRM + PV OF THE TAX SHIELD (Vl = Vu + Debt x Tax rate)
Lower than the value of the unlevered firm, since debt adds greatly to risk
Equal to the value of the unlevered firm

explanation: Interest deductibility adds a tax-shield value; under pure MM with taxes, value keeps rising with debt - tempered in practice by bankruptcy costs.

revisionHistory.question: Under MM WITH corporate taxes, the value of a LEVERED firm is:
options: VALUE OF UNLEVERED FIRM + PV OF THE TAX SHIELD (Vl = Vu + Debt x Tax rate)
revisionHistory.explanation: Interest deductibility adds a tax-shield value; under pure MM with taxes, value keeps rising with debt - tempered in practice by bankruptcy costs.

question: The proposition "the cost of equity is a linear function of the debt-equity ratio" belongs to:

options.text: MM approach (Proposition II) - Ke = Ko + (Ko - Kd)(D/E)
The NI approach of Durand, as propounded by him
The Gordon model of the dividends, as propounded by him
The Walter model of the dividends, as propounded by him

explanation: MM Proposition II: Ke rises linearly with leverage as shareholders demand compensation for financial risk.

revisionHistory.question: The proposition "the cost of equity is a linear function of the debt-equity ratio" belongs to:
options: MM approach (Proposition II) - Ke = Ko + (Ko - Kd)(D/E)
revisionHistory.explanation: MM Proposition II: Ke rises linearly with leverage as shareholders demand compensation for financial risk.

question: ARBITRAGE in the MM model means:

options.text: Trading in the shares of the company with inside information
Hedging of the positions taken by the investors
The merger of the firms in the same industry
Investors sell overpriced (levered) shares and create homemade leverage to buy underpriced (unlevered) shares, equalising values

explanation: Personal (homemade) leverage substitutes for corporate leverage, so levered and unlevered firms cannot sell at different total values.

revisionHistory.question: ARBITRAGE in the MM model means:
options: Investors sell overpriced (levered) shares and create homemade leverage to buy underpriced (unlevered) shares, equalising values
revisionHistory.explanation: Personal (homemade) leverage substitutes for corporate leverage, so levered and unlevered firms cannot sell at different total values.

question: The TRADE-OFF theory of capital structure balances:

options.text: The dividends against the retentions of the profits of the year, as the balance
The cost against the revenue of the business of the year, as the balance
The TAX-SHIELD BENEFIT of debt against the COSTS OF FINANCIAL DISTRESS/bankruptcy
The assets against the liabilities of the firm, as on the date, as the balance

explanation: Firms add debt until the marginal tax advantage equals the marginal expected distress cost - an interior optimum.

revisionHistory.question: The TRADE-OFF theory of capital structure balances:
options: The TAX-SHIELD BENEFIT of debt against the COSTS OF FINANCIAL DISTRESS/bankruptcy
revisionHistory.explanation: Firms add debt until the marginal tax advantage equals the marginal expected distress cost - an interior optimum.

question: The PECKING ORDER theory (Myers) ranks financing preference as:

options.text: Any order at all, as the management may please from time to time in the year of the finance
The debt first, then the equity, and the retained earnings last of all in the order
INTERNAL FUNDS (retained earnings) first, then DEBT, and NEW EQUITY LAST (due to information asymmetry)
The equity first, then the debt, and the retained earnings last of all in the order

options.text: The ARR of the project, as the accounting rate of return earned on the investment over its life
The earnings/cash inflows generated AFTER the payback period - IGNORED by the payback method
The total profit earned by the project
Zero in the case of every project

explanation: The payback method cuts off at recovery; later inflows (post-payback profitability) are invisible to it - its classic weakness.

question: The inventory turnover ratio is computed as:

options.text: COST OF GOODS SOLD / AVERAGE INVENTORY
The sales of the year divided by the closing stock of the year
The purchases of the year divided by the closing stock of the year
The sales of the year divided by the average inventory of the year

explanation: Inventory turnover = COGS / average inventory; using sales inflates it by the profit margin.
